assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED opened a genuinely new regime: strong coupling of a single artificial atom to a single microwave photon on a chip, with a controllable, engineerable Hamiltonian. It underlies dispersive readout, resonator-mediated qubit coupling and essentially all present superconducting quantum processors, and it seeded on-chip microwave quantum optics (waveguide QED, photon routing, giant atoms). The discovery is a new quantum-optical platform, not merely an application.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the 2004 strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff et al., Schoelkopf group) are tightly linked. A fair three-person configuration is the experimental pair plus the lead theorist; Girvin's role as senior theory partner is the main competing claim, and credit between Blais and Girvin is not cleanly separable from the supplied text.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and extended in many laboratories for two decades; the interpretation is stable and the field is large. Timely, though the 2025 prize already recognised superconducting-circuit quantum behaviour, so the committee must be sure this is distinct and not a near-repeat.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits may be judged too close.
I work in this field and am close to groups involved, so I flag a possible conflict of interest and potential bias.
Whether Girvin should replace Blais among the three is unresolved.
Parallel contributions to superconducting circuits are outside this candidate's named credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1995 Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions gave a physically concrete route to quantum computing, followed by the broader program of quantum simulation with atoms, ions and lattices. Originality and lasting influence are very high and it shaped both experiment and theory in AMO physics and quantum information.
assessment.attribution: The two names are the clear, long-standing joint credit for the central theoretical proposals, so a two-laureate configuration is clean. Experimental realisations (Wineland, Blatt, Monroe and others) are partly already recognised (Wineland, 2012) or lie outside this candidate's credit.
assessment.maturity: The proposals were demonstrated experimentally soon after and confirmed in many laboratories; the program is mature. Recognition is arguably overdue for theory that has been fully vindicated.
uncertainties: Nobel tradition favours experimental discovery over theory; the committee must be comfortable rewarding a proposal, though widely validated.
The same two names are credited in B026, so the prize motivation needs careful framing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, through Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's record-accuracy realisation, transformed timekeeping, enabled tests of fundamental constants and relativity at the centimetre level, and are preparing a redefinition of the second. This is a clean, well-controlled demonstration of a new capability grounded in quantum physics.
assessment.attribution: Katori originated the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye is the leading experimental developer, so two names give a fair configuration. Related precision-spectroscopy and ion-clock work was recognised in 2005 and 2012 and is separate. Ye's appearance in several candidacies (B010) adds a minor allocation question.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed in many national metrology institutes, with clock agreement at the 10^-18 level; well established, timely and unlikely to be overturned.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes in precision spectroscopy and ion clocks.
Jun Ye's role across several candidacies could complicate the allocation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and the theory of fault-tolerant, topological quantum computation established that large-scale quantum computation is possible in principle, and directly underlie the experimental effort in superconducting and other platforms. As someone working to make qubits good enough to compute with, I regard this as foundational; surface codes are now being tested in hardware.
assessment.attribution: Shor's code (1995) and Steane's code (1996) are founding results, while Kitaev's fault-tolerant anyon proposal is distinct and arguably the most original. Others (Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Preskill, Zurek) have strong claims, so the three-person configuration is contentious and may be unfair.
assessment.maturity: Below-threshold logical-qubit experiments are recent and still few; the theory is mature but its physical vindication is only beginning. The topological part may be slightly premature.
uncertainties: Many plausible co-contributors fall outside the credited names, so the selection of three is disputable.
Whether this counts as physics rather than mathematics and computer science for Nobel purposes.
Experimental confirmation of scalable fault tolerance is not yet independent or broad; I would avoid hype.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling mechanical oscillators to their quantum ground state and controlling them with light or microwaves extended quantum mechanics to macroscopic objects through ground-state cooling, squeezing, entanglement of motion and quantum transduction. The superconducting-circuit demonstration of a mechanical quantum ground state by Cleland and colleagues is especially clean.
assessment.attribution: Cleland is credited with the first mechanical quantum ground state and quantum control with a qubit; Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer drove cavity optomechanics including sideband cooling. Others (Teufel, Lehnert, Painter, Harris, Schwab) made equally decisive demonstrations, so allocation of credit is a real problem.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by several groups on different platforms and the picture is stable, though applications are still developing. Reasonably timely, but broadly distributed credit makes a three-person prize difficult.
uncertainties: Credit is spread among many groups and the three names omit key contributors.
Whether this is a single clear advance or a set of related ones that need a fitting prize motivation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade and programmable neutral-atom tweezer arrays provide a platform for quantum simulation and increasingly for quantum computing, enabling exploration of new many-body phases and high-fidelity gates. The impact is clear and growing quickly.
assessment.attribution: Blockade proposals (Jaksch, Cirac, Zoller, Lukin and others) and early blockade demonstrations (Saffman, Grangier, Browaeys) make credit complex. The supplied list has four names, so any trio drops one major contributor, and array programmability is partly the work of others outside the credited set.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across groups, but the field is moving fast and the final form of the discovery (computation versus simulation) is not settled, so it may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Logical-qubit and fault-tolerance results are recent.
Attribution is among the hardest in the list, with contributors missing from the credited names.
Distinguishing the blockade discovery from the array technology.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Loss-DiVincenzo proposal for spin qubits in quantum dots and the subsequent experimental demonstrations of single-spin control and readout, including high-fidelity silicon devices, established a leading solid-state qubit platform compatible with semiconductor manufacturing. The physics is of high quality and experimental progress is clear.
assessment.attribution: Loss and DiVincenzo made the 1998 proposal and Vandersypen led key experimental realisations, but other groups (Kouwenhoven, Marcus, Yacoby, Petta, Tarucha, Morello, Dzurak) made major contributions, so experimental credit is spread and weakens the case for a single experimentalist.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed across multiple groups and materials with high gate fidelities in silicon and germanium; the platform is mature in principle, although scalable computation is not demonstrated.
uncertainties: Experimental credit is distributed among many groups beyond the three named.
The decisive advances may be seen as engineering progress rather than a single discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and the entanglement-based E91) turned quantum foundations into a practical protocol and a research field of its own. It is conceptually elegant and has led to commercial and satellite implementations, with clear long-term significance for quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (1984) and Ekert (1991) are the usual trio; the credited discovery is theoretical, and Wiesner (conjugate coding) has an acknowledged historical claim. Experimental realisations are credited elsewhere.
assessment.maturity: The concept has been stable for decades and demonstrated in many laboratories, so the application is well established. Recognition is plausible now, though the 2022 entanglement prize partly covers the underlying physics.
uncertainties: The 2022 prize on entangled photons and Bell tests overlaps in subject matter.
Whether a protocol proposal, as opposed to a physical discovery, is the right target; Wiesner's claim lies outside the credited names.
